body.text: “There are no instructions to hold back and no instructions not to use all the weapons available to the domestic security forces”: Laurent Nunez, Interior Minister of France, October 2, 2026.

What does the above statement, boldly declared on national TV by a senior member of the current French government, tell us about France this autumn of 2026? France: a founder member of the European Union. The continent’s second biggest economy after Germany. A crucible of European culture, marked by its language, rich traditions, great scientists and philosophers, and distinctive contributions to art, literature, music, and cinema. If not without its problems, a civilised land. “There are no instructions to hold back….”

Over the past month, the world has been watching an extraordinary wave of state savagery unfold across France. In city after city, the country’s ultra-militarised police, riot squads, and assorted “special forces” have set about their work with extreme zealotry, as if oblivious to the global visibility of their actions. There is palpable glee in the way they have been clobbering protesters and lobbing tear gas canisters at point-blank range. No question of “proportionate” responses or careful assessment of situations. Battle-primed police have been simply letting rip, deploying not just the batons and tear gas of old but also a panoply of “non-lethal” high-velocity weapons: stun grenades which explode on touch, and “flashball” launchers, which propel rubber projectiles at intense velocity into flesh and eye socket.

For many in France, all this has stirred memories of the state suppression of the Gilets Jaunes (Yellow Vest) movement during Emmanuel Macron’s first presidential term (2017–22). The difference—the astounding, difficult-to-get-your-head-around difference—is that this time the target of state wrath is the country’s children.
A grim new school year

In September, schoolchildren across France returned to their classes after the long summer break: the “re-entry” or return to normal rhythms of study, work, and life known here as la rentrée. There is (or used to be) a pleasing rite-of-passage quality to this day, a celebratory sense of stepping into the future, even for children confronting long days ahead of classroom incarceration, homework, and examinations. There is (or used to be) more than a hint of optimism for everyone: teachers, parents, and children.
Long years of austerity, of selling the French education system short while boosting the fortunes of the country’s surging billionaire class, have put paid to that.

For countless numbers of French middle- and high-school children, particularly those in less advantaged areas, the rentrée this autumn has been to schools whose dilapidation screams extreme underfunding. Here, roofs leak, electricity snaps, windows will not close, toilets are beyond inadequate, and rats scuttle about. Here, poorly heated and ventilated classrooms impose icy conditions in winter while turning into 40-degree furnaces during heatwaves. In some instances, there is no drinking water.

On top of this, students once again found themselves at the sharp end of a cynical numbers game: more students per class, fewer teachers to address their needs. Under France’s highly centralised education system, teachers are civil servants whose recruitment, training, and placement are subject to rigid state direction. This gives governments a free hand when it comes to cutting teacher numbers, leaving teaching posts unfilled and bumping up class sizes. For students, the implications are legion: you might suddenly discover there is no one to teach mathematics or that the course you had set your heart on has been summarily withdrawn.

For high school students who, against the odds, successfully negotiate the summit of the French school system, the fabled baccalauréate final exam, there is the trial of somehow finding themselves a university place. Introduced early in the Macron presidency, in 2018, a new allocation system known as the Parcoursup was supposed to inject speed and efficiency into the process of easing candidates into tertiary education. In practice, it has proved calamitous; a month or so ago, 1,26,000 qualified candidates, 50,000 of them fresh out of high school, were still waiting to be assigned university or college places; in Paris, orientation centres are said to be full of “lost” young baccalauréate holders trapped in limbo.

Wretched school buildings; no basic facilities; crowded classrooms; missing teachers; closed roads ahead after a gruelling final examination: the Macron government could not be sending a clearer message about how low this generation figures in its estimation. Small wonder French schoolchildren have had enough.
Political context

For Macron and team, and for the French establishment more generally, the youth uprising has erupted at a particularly unpropitious moment: full square in the run-up to next year’s presidential election. As Macronism, the French variant of neoliberal “extreme centre” politics, lumbers towards its inglorious, unlamented end, two opposing forces are emerging as front runners in the battle to replace it. In one corner, the neo-fascist far-right Rassemblement National (National Rally), led by Marine Le Pen. In the other, an insurgent radical left coalesced around La France Insoumise (LFI; France Unbowed) and its inspirational leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Le Pen currently leads, but to the consternation of the French state, and its ultra-wealthy base, every major opinion poll now has Mélenchon making it through to the second round of next April’s presidential vote, ready to take on Le Pen in a fight-to-the-death duel.

If Le Pen remains the bookie’s favourite, she still faces the indignity of campaigning for the presidency under house arrest and wearing an electronic ankle tag. In July, her 2025 conviction for the embezzlement of close to 3 million euros of EU funds was upheld on appeal, and although her punishment has been scaled back (she was originally awarded a four-year prison term and a five-year ban from holding public office), she enters the presidential race as a convicted felon with form for dodgy financial dealings. Her stand-in, should she decide to stand aside, is Jordan Bardella, the party’s poster boy president and purported fresh new denazified face..

Thanks to some forensic investigative journalism by Mediapart, an independent online news operation, we now know that just 10 years ago, a cocky young Bardella was sharing extreme anti-Semitic material and classic anti-Jewish tropes in emails and via social media. These revelations, which Bardella and Le Pen unwisely continue to deny rather than attribute to youthful indiscretion, have punched a cannon-sized hole through the party’s 15-year-long dédiabolisation (de-demonisation campaign: an effort to persuade voters that its racist and Nazi-endorsing past is at an end).

A combative, confident candidate of the Left already riding high. Against him, a neo-fascist candidate with a criminal record and an openly racist entourage. In between, an assortment of hopefuls, with no clear or appetising contender for the hallowed centre ground. This political conjuncture helps explain several aspects of the French state’s response to its upstart children.

Firstly, it offers context for the ferocity of the response: the state’s impulse to resort to extreme violence, together with judicial fiat, to quell the rebellion quickly. Beat the kids up; conduct mass arrests (over 8,000 thus far, the majority of them involving minors); delegitimise everything they do, from building barricades (a time-honoured tradition in France) to protesting outside their schools. Confiscate their slogan-bearing placards (on social media, you can watch the offending bits of cardboard being grabbed by burly police functionaries bristling with weapons). If, as a result, some of these upstart kids sustain grievous, life-changing injuries—a hand blown off by a grenade, say, or an eye put out, or a jaw shattered, with all the lower teeth ripped out and the prospect of years of reconstructive surgery ahead—well, that is simply collateral damage. These children must be brought to heel, and fast.

A second corollary is the continuing government effort to position the radical left, in particular the LFI, as instigators of the uprising. Assisted by mainstream TV and news outlets, already working flat out to amplify the occasional cases where teenage protesters have taken things too far (the overwhelming majority of protests have been non-violent). The state has been seeking to sell a ludicrous conspiracy whereby LFI leaders, marshalled by a Machiavellian Mélenchon, dart from school to school stirring otherwise placid students to revolt. There are few buyers for a narrative that, as many have pointed out, infantilises school students and denies them agency. If the LFI has made plain its solidarity by attending their rallies, or joining parents, teachers, and trade unionists to form human chains to keep the security goons at bay, the young people are proving well capable of mobilising, organising, and campaigning for a different future, one radically at odds with that planned for them by the powers that be.

This explains the mammoth turnout for the nationwide day of action on October 17. Against mainstream media efforts to portray the schoolchildren’s uprising as running out of steam, something in the order of 8,00,000 people, including parents, grandparents, trade unionists, and veterans of the Yellow Vest movement, took to the streets in overwhelmingly peaceful if boisterous displays of solidarity.

In the days beforehand, the Macron government seemed to shed any lingering vestige of sanity. It lifted the temporary ban on the police use of stun grenades, announced on October 7 by Interior Minister Nuñez following incidents in which minors had sustained crippling, life-changing injuries. As if raring for a confrontation, it refused to approve a sensible, manageable route for the tens of thousands of protesters it knew would mobilise in Paris. As for the country’s quarter-million-strong “law enforcement” operatives, the message from the Élysée Palace could have been set out in neon lights: hit hard; go wild; spare no quarter.
“There are no instructions to hold back….”
On October 17, in Saint-Étienne, another child had his hand blown off by a government-issued grenade.

Susan Ram has spent much of her life viewing the world from different geographical locations. Born in London, she studied politics and international relations before setting off for South Asia: first to Nepal, and then to India, where fieldwork in Tamil Nadu developed into 20 years of residence.
